w: Climb into the sky above Bruges and you're inside the city's original alarm system: this medieval belfry once held the treasury and the municipal archives, and doubled as a lookout scanning for fire and invasion. Still one of the most recognisable towers in Belgium, ringing out over the Markt below.
s: Medieval watchtower still ringing over the Markt
_facts: medieval bell tower in centre of Bruges
formerly housed treasury and municipal archives
served as observation post for fires and other dangers
one of the city's most prominent symbols

w: Its brick tower climbs 115.6 metres over Bruges - the third-tallest brickwork church spire on Earth, and still the tallest thing in town. Flying buttresses raised in the 1270s hold up a Gothic nave, while a 1482 chapel inside was built for the wealthy Lodewijk van Gruuthuse's private worship.
_facts: 115.6m tower, tallest structure in Bruges
third tallest brickwork church tower in the world
Gothic flying buttresses built 1270s-80s
chapel built 1482 for Lodewijk van Gruuthuse

w: Built on the ruins of the medieval Eekhout Abbey, this municipal museum tracks six centuries of Flemish and Belgian painting in one unbroken run - from Jan van Eyck's Early Netherlandish panels through Renaissance and Baroque masters to Belgian symbolism, Flemish Expressionism, and Marcel Broodthaers' postwar work.
s: Six centuries of Flemish painting on one abbey site
_facts: built on site of medieval Eekhout Abbey
collection spans Jan van Eyck to Marcel Broodthaers
includes Early Netherlandish, Renaissance, Baroque, symbolism, Expressionism

w: Bruges' cathedral carries two names - the Cathedral of the Saviour and St Donat - and a double dedication: to the 'risen saviour' (Verrezen Zaligmaker, echoing the Latin salvator) and to Saint-Donatius of Reims, whose relics anchor the Roman Catholic seat of the city.
_facts: Roman Catholic cathedral of Bruges
also known as Cathedral of the Saviour and St. Donat
dedicated to the 'risen saviour' and Saint-Donatius of Reims

w: Dutch for exactly what it is: Bruges' central square, barely a hectare of cobbles, has anchored the city centre for centuries. The 13th-century Belfry looms over its south side - one of Belgium's most photographed skylines, seen from ground level.
s: Bruges' beating heart, one hectare wide
_facts: central square of Bruges, about 1 hectare
located in the city centre
13th-century Belfry stands on its south side

w: The last of Bruges' beguinages, and the only one still standing: communities of pious laywomen filled these whitewashed houses for centuries. The beguines are gone now - Benedictine nuns took over in 1927, founded by canon Hoornaert, renaming the priory Monasterium De Wijngaard, and still live behind its walls today.
s: Bruges' last beguinage, now a Benedictine priory
_facts: only preserved beguinage in Bruges
no beguines remain; Benedictine convent since 1927
founded by canon Hoornaert
houses reshaped into Monasterium De Wijngaard priory

w: Sick pilgrims were tended here from the mid-12th century, making this one of Europe's oldest surviving hospital buildings. Victorian planners wanted it demolished in the 1860s; Gothic Revival enthusiasts saved it instead. It stopped treating patients in 1977, and now holds the Hans Memling museum.
_facts: medieval hospital founded mid-12th century
among Europe's oldest surviving hospital buildings
1860s demolition plan blocked by Gothic Revival supporters
ceased hospital use in 1977
now houses Hans Memling museum
